top.h1: How many people died in Pompeii, and did anyone survive?
answer: About 2,000 people died inside Pompeii's walls,
, and the remains of more than 1,000 have been found. The town had perhaps
people, so most had left, and
has traced at least 172 survivors by name.
top.strength: Remains found: counted by the excavators. The dead inside the walls and the townspeople: estimates. The dead outside the town: not known.

slot.what: The people of Pompeii and the dead found inside the town, to one scale. How many died on the roads and shores outside is not known.
slot.alt: A bar chart to one scale. Pompeii's people, perhaps 11,000 to 20,000, drawn dashed as an estimate. The dead inside the walls, about 2,000 by the archaeological park's estimate, also dashed. The remains of 1,044 people counted at Pompeii by 2003, drawn solid: 394 in the pumice fall and 650 in the hot surges. The rest of the town left, or died outside it, and was never counted. Below, at the same scale, the remains of about 300 people counted on the shore of Herculaneum, the smaller town nearby, by 2018.

faq.a: From one witness across the bay, from the digs and the bones, and from names cut in stone.

paras: Yes, many did, perhaps most of the town. Scholars now broadly agree that much, "perhaps even a majority", of the people of Pompeii and Herculaneum probably survived, Steven Tuck writes in
, his book of 2025.
on the town from the early afternoon of the first day into the early hours of the next, so there were hours in which to leave.
Tuck has traced at least 172 survivors by name, "probably representing about 3,000 household members". He looked for family names known at Pompeii and Herculaneum that turn up after the eruption on
. Most settled on the coast from Naples to Cumae, others at Capua, Nola or as far as Ostia.
Some came back.

that people lived in the ruins again after the eruption, in two phases, the last in the 4th and 5th centuries. For anyone with nowhere else to go, its archaeologists write, it was better than nothing.

At Herculaneum, the smaller town nearby, about 300 people had taken refuge in twelve vaults on the shore and died there when the first hot surge came,

blocks.nav: When and how did they die?
blocks.h: When and how did they die?
paras: Over about a day, in two phases. By 2003, 1,044 dead had been counted at Pompeii, besides

of about 100 more. Of them, 394 lay in the pumice that fell through the first afternoon and night, nine in ten of them inside buildings, probably where roofs and floors gave way. The other 650 lay in the deposits of the hot surges that reached the town the next morning, as
sets out.
How exactly they died is argued. The 2010 study found that heat, at least 250 °C even 10 kilometres from the vent, was the main cause of death, against the older view that people choked on the ash.
that anyone still in the city "died at once of thermal shock". At Herculaneum,
found that soft tissue and the stone vaults had shielded the bones from part of the heat, and it calls the exact manner of death there still unclear.
Even the day is open. Pliny's letter gives 24 August in all its oldest manuscripts, some finds point to the autumn, and
declines to name a winner.

blocks.nav: How many people lived in Pompeii?
blocks.h: How many people lived in Pompeii?
paras: Perhaps 11,000 to 20,000. No count of the people survives, so every figure is worked back from what the town left behind, and scholars differ. A count from the households gives about 11,000, the
reports, while
gives at least 20,000. Herculaneum was smaller, with perhaps
to
people.
From one witness across the bay, from the digs and the bones, and from names cut in stone.
No one in Pompeii left an account. The nearest is Pliny the Younger's: he watched the eruption from Misenum, across the bay, and described it some 25 years later, by the usual dating, in

to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, took the fleet out to help people on the shore and died at Stabiae (letter 6.16). In letter 6.20 Pliny tells of the crowd fleeing with him in the dark: women wailing, small children crying, men shouting, people calling for parents, children and wives and knowing them by their voices.

since the 18th century, and the layer each person lay in shows when they died. At Herculaneum, the skeletons on the shore have been studied since the 1980s, the 2018 study notes: men, women and children of the town. Names on inscriptions trace the survivors. And some of the dead left no heirs at all: the emperor Titus gave their property to rebuild the stricken towns, Suetonius writes (Titus 8.4, quoted in
What stays open is how many lived in the town, how many died on the roads and shores, and on which day. The chart above draws the estimates dashed and leaves the uncounted dead without a number.

paras: Nothing turned to stone: the bodies decayed inside the hardened ash and left hollows, and from 1863 plaster was poured into some of them to make casts.
Most of the town had left before the end, and at least 172 survivors are known by name.
The dying went on for about a day: first under the pumice and the falling roofs, then in the surges of the next morning.
The survivors Tuck traced were rich and poor, men, women and children, "a cross section of the population".
That date goes back to a book of 1929 that used the manuscripts wrongly, the park's study of 2024 says. Pliny's letter gives 24 August, some finds point to the autumn, and the day is still argued.
